Let me understand the rule. The verifier: finds objects (univalued=False, diagonal=False, without_bg=True). Then gets colors of objects. Then x3 = lbind(sfilter, x2) — wait sfilter(container, condition). lbind(sfilter, x2) fixes container=x2, returns lambda condition: sfilter(x2, condition). x4 = lbind(matcher, identity) = matcher(identity, target) -> lambda target: matcher(identity, target) = lambda target: lambda x: identity(x)==target.

x5 = chain(size, x3, x4) = lambda x: size(x3(x4(x))). Hmm chain(h,g,f) = h(g(f(x))). So x5(x) = size(x3(x4(x))). x4(x) = matcher(identity, x) = lambda y: y == x. x3(cond) = sfilter(x2, cond) = colors equal to x. size = count of colors equal to x. So x5(x) = number of objects whose color == x.

x6 = matcher(x5, ONE) = lambda x: x5(x) == 1. x7 = sfilter(x2, x6) = colors x in x2 such that number of objects with that color == 1.

x8 = lbind(colorcount, I) = lambda value: colorcount(I, value). x9 = argmax(x7, x8) = color among those appearing in exactly one object with maximum count in grid.

x10 = matcher(color, x9) = lambda obj: color(obj)==x9. x11 = extract(x0, x10) = the object with that color. x12 = subgrid(x11, I) = crop.

So output is the bounding-box subgrid of the unique object whose color is unique (appears in exactly one object) and has the most cells.

In the example, color 6 forms a block. Output is bounding box crop of 6-object. Note output includes a 0 at top-right because the bounding box of the 6 shape includes a background cell.

So the dense block color 6 appears once. Output = crop of bounding box.
